title: Scipio's small bath
hook: Seneca visits Scipio's plain country house and its tiny dark bath (Letters 86)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the honey you make yourself. Your line was one sound rises. Did you blend two ideas into a sentence of your own, and name where each came from? Day four hundred seventy-six.

Scipio Africanus was the Roman general who beat Hannibal, the man Seneca calls the terror of Carthage. After all of it, he left Rome and went to live on a farm at Liternum, on the coast. Long afterward, Seneca goes there and stays in Scipio's own house. He looks over the stone walls and the towers, and then he finds the bath. It's tiny, and dark, and he's delighted. The eighty-sixth letter is a tour, and a little sermon on plumbing. Today, the last day of this week in the letters: Scipio's small bath.
screen: `THE GENERAL WHO BEAT HANNIBAL.` → `A FARM AT LITERNUM.` → `A BATH, TINY AND DARK.`

segments.voice: First, the house. Built of squared stone, with a wall around a wood, and towers at both ends. Seneca says he's lying in the very house of Scipio as he writes, and that he has paid his respects at what people say is Scipio's tomb. Second, the bath. Small, narrow, and dark, in the old style, Seneca says: the old Romans didn't think a bath was warm unless it was dim. Here the man who terrified Carthage washed a body tired from farm work, under this cheap roof, on this plain floor. Third, the contrast. Now, Seneca says, people feel poor unless their walls shine with big precious mirrors, unless their pools are lined with marble, unless water pours from silver taps. In Scipio's bath there were slits rather than windows. Now, Seneca says, people sneer at any bath that doesn't take in the sun all day through huge windows. Fourth, what's enough. Seneca isn't telling anyone to bathe in the dark. His point is that the great man of Rome needed very little, and lost nothing by it. Looking back on our week, from Attalus's old wine and school in old age to the stage kings, the honest timetable and the bees, the thread is plainness: honest memory, honest days, honest pleasure. Plain was enough for Scipio.
screen: `SCIPIO'S HOUSE AT LITERNUM.` · `A SMALL, DARK BATH.` · `NOW EVERYONE WANTS MIRRORS.` · `THE GREAT MAN NEEDED LITTLE.` · then, large: `PLAIN WAS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Choose one plain thing near you right now: a glass of water, a slice of bread, the chair you're sitting in, the light through a window. Give it your full attention, as if it were the bath of a hero. Notice its texture, its weight, its use. Let it be enough, just for this minute. If a wish for something fancier rises, let it pass, and come back to the plain thing. The bell holds the time.
Balneolum. Latin for a little bath: Scipio Africanus washed in one, narrow and dark, after farm work, and Seneca says it was enough. Today's word.

Your line: plain was enough. Enjoy one plain thing today, fully, without upgrading it. That's our week in the letters. Next week, Seneca on learning and on living together. Day four hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Some people inspired by Seneca keep one part of their life deliberately plain, a meal, a room or a routine, and take pleasure in it rather than in upgrades.

myth: Scipio's bath was large and bright with windows
it was small and dark, with only slits for light.
Seneca says old Romans thought a bath warm only if it was dim
the darkness was part of the old style.
Seneca tells everyone to bathe in the dark
his point is that the great man needed little and lost nothing by it.

fork.setup: you're staying in a hero's old farmhouse, and the bath is a tiny dark cell. what does Seneca feel?
options: delight: the man who beat Carthage washed here, and it was enough.
fork.reveal: Seneca praises the plain bath and contrasts it with the mirrored, marble baths of his own day.

original.note: Latin: a little bath. Seneca, Letters 86.4, describes Scipio's as narrow and dark in the old style.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about old plumbing.
what it means: the man who beat Hannibal lived plainly, and plain was enough.
what a scholar hears: Letters 86.1–13; Scipio Africanus (died c. 183 BCE) retired to Liternum; Seneca also tells of planting olive trees there with the farmer Aegialus (86.14–21).

notes: Letters 86.1: Seneca writes lying in Scipio's villa, having visited his tomb (or the altar people take for his tomb). 86.4: the house of squared stone, walls around a wood, towers; 'balneolum angustum, tenebricosum ex consuetudine antiqua'. 86.5: Scipio washing a body tired from farm work. 86.6–8: contemporary luxury (mirrors, marble, silver taps); 86.8: such baths now called caves ('cavernas'). Confirm details.
'Some two and a half centuries later': Scipio died c. 183 BCE; Letters 86 c. 64 CE, about 245 years. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'saved Rome' and 'one of the greatest heroes the city ever had' (unsourced superlatives) and 'two and a half centuries later' (a count the letter doesn't give); cut the invented 'small stone rooms'. 86.8 does not call such baths 'caves' (the jeer there is at baths without huge sunny windows, 'blattaria'); fixed. The week look-back wrongly included day 469 (last week) and skipped 472–473; corrected. 'Beat Hannibal' is standard history, not stated in Letter 86; Seneca's own phrase is 'horror Carthaginis' (86.5).
